## Simple explanation

Unsupervised learning looks for patterns in data that does not come with
target answers. It can group similar examples, compress data, or discover
representations that may be useful for later tasks.

## Technical explanation

Unsupervised methods optimize objectives based on input data without
supervised target labels. Examples include clustering, density estimation,
dimensionality reduction, and some self-supervised representation-learning
methods. “Unsupervised” covers a broad range of objectives and assumptions.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Labels can be expensive or unavailable, while large collections of raw
data may be accessible. Unsupervised structure can support exploration,
anomaly detection, and pretraining, but discovered groups do not
automatically correspond to meaningful real-world categories.

## How it works

An algorithm uses similarity, reconstruction, likelihood, or another
data-derived objective to organize or represent examples. Engineers assess
the output using domain review, stability checks, downstream tasks, or
appropriate intrinsic metrics.

## Practical example

A team can cluster support tickets using text embeddings to explore common
themes before defining a supervised routing taxonomy. Human review is
needed to decide whether the clusters are coherent and useful.

## Common misconceptions

- Unsupervised learning does not mean the algorithm makes no assumptions;
  its representation, objective, and hyperparameters shape results.
- Clusters are not automatically true classes or causal categories.
